conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you came in today with a sore throat, eye irritation, and a rash. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had a sore throat for about three days, and my neck glands feel swollen. My eyes are red and itchy, especially around the lids. I think there’s a rash near my mouth, but the nurse didn’t see it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, cough, or runny nose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I haven’t had a fever or cold symptoms. Just the sore throat, eyes, and this itchiness on my chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of stem cell transplant, we’re concerned this could be graft-versus-host disease, or GVHD. We’ll run some tests to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: GVHD again? I thought I was past that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Chronic GVHD can flare up even months later. We’ll check your tacrolimus level—it helps prevent GVHD—and we’ll also look for infections like herpes or viruses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking my meds, but I did stop INH recently because of stomach pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That might explain the stomach issues, but not these new symptoms. We’ll keep monitoring. For now, we’ll admit you for observation and testing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CMV and respiratory virus tests came back negative. No flu, RSV, or adenovirus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a cold or flu?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. That makes GVHD more likely. We’re going to do a skin biopsy today to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a small pinch with local numbing. It’s quick, and it’ll help us know how to treat you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy is done. We sent the sample to pathology. Results should be back in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My throat still hurts, and now I feel some sores inside my mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed white patches in your mouth. ENT looked and didn’t see ulcers, but we’re concerned it might be herpes. We’ll start you on valacyclovir just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the throat swab was negative for HSV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but sometimes swabs miss it. Since you’ve had transplants, we don’t want to take chances. We’ll treat for 7 days and then go back to your usual acyclovir.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your eye doctor saw you yesterday. They think your eye symptoms are due to GVHD. We’re starting lubricating drops and ointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The drops help a little, but my eyes still burn.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll increase the ointment to four times a day. It should soothe them more, especially at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are a bit high. We’re not sure why yet—could be GVHD, meds, or something else. We’ll monitor them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. They’re only mildly elevated, and we’ve seen this before in transplant patients. We’ll repeat the labs and see if they improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The skin biopsy came back. It shows changes consistent with GVHD—interface dermatitis with apoptosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s definitely GVHD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The pathologist ruled out a viral rash. We’ll start topical steroids—clobetasol for your torso, triamcinolone for your neck, and tacrolimus ointment for your face.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more steroids by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your prednisone to 20mg in the morning and 15mg at night. It’ll help control the GVHD flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t like being on high steroids. I gained weight last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll use the lowest effective dose and taper it as soon as you improve. This is temporary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You developed a cough with yellow sputum. We did a chest CT—no pneumonia or fluid. It’s likely just irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s not serious then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The scan shows your lungs are clear. The old spot in your upper lobe has even improved. We won’t treat unless it worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your cough is better today. That’s good. The sputum culture just showed normal mouth bacteria, so no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my abdominal pain? It’s still there, same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your history—it’s been chronic. We’ll get a CT of your abdomen to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The abdominal CT is back—completely normal. No inflammation, blockage, or fluid. Your pain is likely related to prior GVHD or nerve sensitivity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing to do about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep managing it with pain meds. It hasn’t gotten worse, so that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver tests are trending down. That’s a good sign. We’re still ruling out hepatitis, but so far, everything looks okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my tacrolimus level?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was low. That might have contributed to the GVHD flare. We’re increasing your dose to 1mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need blood tests to check it again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll monitor it regularly to keep it in the right range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your eye symptoms are still bothering you. We’re increasing the artificial tears to every two hours during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a lot of drops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But dry eyes from GVHD can get worse if not treated well. We want to protect your vision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Big improvements today. Your rash is less red, your throat feels better, and your eyes are less irritated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. We’ll give you prescriptions for the creams, eye drops, and valacyclovir for seven days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay on 20mg in the morning and 15mg at night for now. Your transplant team will help taper it slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tacrolimus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Now 1mg twice daily. Keep taking it exactly as prescribed to prevent more flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the nystatin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, four times a day. It’s to prevent mouth fungus, especially with the steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re discharging you today. Keep using all the creams and eye treatments as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with my transplant doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and call us if you develop fever, trouble eating, or any new symptoms. You’ve done great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest and take it easy at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your liver enzymes are still a bit high but improving. Your transplant team will monitor them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. It’s likely related to GVHD or meds. As long as they keep trending down, we’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in clinic soon. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember—artificial tears every two hours while awake, and lacrilube four times a day, especially at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll set reminders.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. That’ll help keep your eyes comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad this flare is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So are we. You responded well to treatment. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you in clinic.
